questions.q: Per this lesson, why does it make sense for metadata itself to have quality dimensions?
options: Because metadata is itself a kind of data, so it can have the same kinds of quality problems the data it describes has
Because metadata is stored in a completely different format than all other data
Because only technical metadata can ever have quality problems
Because Data Quality Management's dimensions only apply to financial data
questions.explain: This directly follows Lesson 1's premise that metadata is data that describes other data — it's not exempt from the same quality concerns.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the four metadata-specific quality dimensions named in this lesson?
options: Coverage — what percentage of objects have any metadata at all
The physical color of the server rack
The number of letters in the table's name
The database vendor's stock price
questions.explain: The four dimensions are coverage, freshness, correctness, and consistency — each paralleling a Data Quality Management dimension, applied to metadata instead of data.

questions.q: In the worked IsActiveFlag example, why is the 'correctness failure' described as more dangerous than the 'coverage failure'?
options: The correctness failure is silent — it looks complete, but is actually wrong, while the coverage failure is obvious and easy to spot
The coverage failure is actually worse in every case
Both failures are described as equally harmless
Correctness failures can never actually happen in a real catalog
questions.explain: An empty description field is an obvious gap; a description that looks complete but no longer matches reality (after the business redefined 'active' from 90 to 60 days) gives false confidence with no visible warning sign.

questions.q: Which Data Quality Management dimension does this lesson say 'freshness' most directly parallels?
options: Timeliness
Uniqueness
Validity
Accuracy
questions.explain: Freshness — how old the 'last reviewed' date is — is this course's version of the timeliness problem covered in Data Quality Management, Lesson 16.

questions.q: What does this lesson suggest as a simple, practical way to measure catalog-wide metadata quality?
options: A scorecard tracking the percentage of columns with descriptions (coverage) and recent review dates (freshness), reviewed quarterly
Deleting every entry that hasn't been edited in the last 24 hours
Hiring a new database administrator for every single table
Disabling the catalog's search function entirely
questions.explain: Even a rough scorecard, checked periodically, turns 'we think our catalog is decent' into an actual trackable number.
